title: THEY NAMED HIM PAIN… BUT GOD REFUSED TO LET PAIN WRITE HIS FINAL CHAPTER
paragraphs: THEY NAMED HIM PAIN… BUT GOD REFUSED TO LET PAIN WRITE HIS FINAL CHAPTER
Who Was Jabez, the Man Whose Prayer Interrupted a Genealogy? — The forgotten man in 1 Chronicles 4:9–10 whose two-verse story reveals what happens when a wounded life reaches for the living God.
Some people are born into a family name.
Others are born into a family wound.
And sometimes, before you are old enough to understand what happened to you, somebody has already decided what your life is going to mean.
Maybe they called you a disappointment.
Maybe you grew up hearing that you were a mistake.
Maybe nobody actually said those words, but the way they treated you made the message painfully clear.
You were the difficult child. The unwanted pregnancy. The one who never measured up. The person who always seemed to bring trouble into the room.
And somewhere along the way, you stopped questioning the label.
You started living inside it.
But buried in one of the most easily skipped sections of the Bible is a man whose name carried the memory of pain.
His name was Jabez.
And what Scripture says about him takes only two verses.
Two verses.
No dramatic account of armies falling. No record of a sea splitting open. No detailed biography explaining his childhood, his failures, his relationships, or his accomplishments.
Just a name.
A wound.
A prayer.
And an answer from God.
Yet there is something extraordinary about where his story appears.
The writer of 1 Chronicles is tracing generations. Names follow names. Families follow families. The record moves forward through the history of God's covenant people.
Then, suddenly, the narrative slows.
A man named Jabez steps into view.
And for two remarkable verses, the genealogy becomes a testimony.

If you have ever wondered whether God sees you when your life feels ordinary, whether your painful beginning has already determined your ending, or whether your prayers still matter after years of disappointment, stay with this story.
Because the most important thing about Jabez was not the pain attached to his name.
It was the God he called upon.
And the difference between those two truths may change the way you understand your own life.
The Bible introduces him this way:
“Jabez was more honourable than his brethren: and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, Because I bare him with sorrow.”
— 1 Chronicles 4:9, KJV
Read that again.
His mother named him Jabez because she bore him in sorrow.
In Hebrew, the name appears as יַעְבֵּץ (Yaʿbēṣ), commonly transliterated Jabez.
The verse connects his name with the Hebrew word עֹצֶב (ʿōṣeb), meaning pain or sorrow, through a deliberate wordplay.
His name became associated with the suffering surrounding his birth.
But notice something important.
Scripture does not tell us exactly why his mother suffered.
Perhaps it involved a difficult delivery. Perhaps there were painful circumstances surrounding his birth. The text does not explain.
We must not turn possibilities into biblical facts.
What we do know is that his name preserved the memory of sorrow.
Imagine growing up carrying a name that reminded people of pain.
Imagine hearing it called across the courtyard.
At the family table.
Among relatives.
Every time someone said his name, the association remained.
Pain.
Sorrow.
Distress.
Some of us understand that more deeply than we want to admit.
Our names may not literally mean pain, but we carry memories that have become identities.
The marriage that collapsed.
The addiction that nearly destroyed us.
The child we lost.
The betrayal we never saw coming.
The mistake everyone remembers.
The season when we walked away from God and wondered whether we could ever come home.
And the terrible thing about shame is that it does not merely remind you of what happened.
It tries to convince you that what happened is who you are.
But the Bible does something fascinating before recording Jabez's prayer.
It tells us that he was more honorable than his brothers.
Not more famous.
Not necessarily wealthier.
Not more powerful.
More honorable.
The Hebrew word translated “honourable” is נִכְבָּד (nikhbād), related to the root כבד (k-b-d), which carries ideas of weight, honor, and significance.
The writer does not give us enough information to explain every reason for that description.
But the contrast is unmistakable.
His name was associated with pain.
His character was associated with honor.
And that distinction matters.
Because the circumstances surrounding your beginning do not automatically determine the character of your life.
Your parents' failures do not have to become your convictions.
The cruelty you experienced does not have to become the cruelty you practice.
The darkness you inherited does not have to be the darkness you pass down.
By God's grace, a different way of living is possible.
Jabez was not introduced as a man without pain.
He was introduced as a man whose life could not be reduced to it.
And then came the prayer.

“And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested.”
— 1 Chronicles 4:10, KJV
There it is.
One prayer.
Four closely connected requests.
And a final sentence so simple that we might miss its significance.
“God granted him that which he requested.”
But before we rush to turn this prayer into a formula for financial success, we need to understand what Jabez was actually saying.
Because this is where a beautiful biblical passage has sometimes been reduced to something much smaller than its original meaning.
Jabez was not handing God a business plan.
He was calling upon the God of Israel.
That distinction changes everything.
The Hebrew begins:
וַיִּקְרָא יַעְבֵּץ לֵאלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
Vayyiqrāʾ Yaʿbēṣ lēʾlōhê Yiśrāʾēl.
“And Jabez called upon the God of Israel.”
He did not address an anonymous force.
He did not appeal to the universe.
He did not attempt to manipulate supernatural power through the correct combination of words.
He called upon the God who had made covenant promises to Israel.
The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
The God who had delivered His people from slavery.
The God whose faithfulness was greater than the failures of those who belonged to Him.
And that is where his prayer begins.
Not with confidence in himself.
But with dependence upon God.
“Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed…”
The Hebrew expression includes:
אִם־בָּרֵךְ תְּבָרֲכֵנִי
ʾIm-bārēkh təvā­răkhēnî.
The repetition of the Hebrew verb for blessing gives the request emphasis.
Jabez is earnestly asking God to bless him.
But blessing in Scripture cannot be reduced to having more money, acquiring a larger house, or enjoying a trouble-free life.
God's blessing can include material provision. Scripture does not deny that.
Yet the biblical understanding of blessing is far richer.
It includes God's favor, His provision, His covenant faithfulness, and the good He gives according to His wisdom.
Sometimes God's blessing comes through an open door.
Sometimes it comes through the strength to remain faithful when the door stays closed.
Sometimes it comes through provision.
Sometimes through correction.
Sometimes through an answered request.
And sometimes through a grace that teaches us to endure what we desperately wanted removed.
The apostle Paul prayed three times for his thorn in the flesh to be taken away.
The Lord's answer was:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
— 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Think about that.
Jabez received what he requested.
Paul did not receive the removal he requested.
Yet both accounts reveal the goodness of God.
One demonstrates God's generosity in granting a petition.
The other demonstrates God's sustaining grace when a petition is not granted in the way we desire.
That is why we must never tell a suffering believer that an unanswered prayer automatically proves a lack of faith.
Some of the most faithful people in Scripture suffered deeply.
And the most important blessing God gives us is not a life in which nothing hurts.
It is the gift of belonging to Him.
Jabez continued:
“...and enlarge my coast…”
The Hebrew expression is:
וְהִרְבִּיתָ אֶת־גְּבוּלִי
Vəhirbîtā ʾet-gəvûlî.
It refers to increasing or enlarging his border or territory.
In the historical setting of ancient Israel, land and boundaries were concrete realities, connected with inheritance, livelihood, and the life of the covenant community.
Jabez was asking for an enlargement of his territory.
We should not pretend the verse originally meant increasing social media followers, expanding a ministry platform, or multiplying a business.
Those may be modern applications people consider, but they are not the literal meaning of the Hebrew text.
And yet the passage does invite us to examine something deeply personal.
What are we asking God to enlarge?
Our influence?
Our possessions?
Our opportunities?
Or our capacity to honor Him with whatever He entrusts to us?
Because there is a dangerous kind of expansion.
A person can gain a larger platform and lose their integrity.
Build a successful business and neglect their family.
Acquire more possessions and become less generous.
Receive greater influence and slowly begin loving applause more than truth.
Not everything that grows is becoming spiritually healthy.
Jesus asked a question that should disturb every heart chasing success without surrender:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
— Mark 8:36, KJV
Jabez asked for more territory.
But the Christian reading his prayer today must remember that our greatest calling is not territorial expansion.
It is faithfulness to Jesus Christ.
We can ask God to enlarge our opportunities to serve, our generosity, our usefulness, and our witness.
But we must submit those desires to His will.
Because a bigger life is not necessarily a better life.
A life surrendered to Christ is.
Then Jabez prayed something that deserves more attention than it often receives.
“...and that thine hand might be with me…”
Not simply, “Give me more.”
But, “Let Your hand be with me.”
In the Old Testament, God's hand can signify His power and active involvement, including His help, protection, and judgment according to the context.
Here, Jabez is asking for God's sustaining presence and assistance.
And suddenly the prayer becomes more than a request for changed circumstances.
It becomes a confession of dependence.
What good would larger territory be if he lived apart from the God who gave it?
What good would a blessing be if it became an excuse to forget the Blesser?
What good would an answered prayer be if the answer eventually became an idol?
There are people who have everything they once begged God to give them.
And they are still empty.
They have the promotion.
The house.
The recognition.
The relationships.
The money.
Yet somewhere between receiving the gift and enjoying the gift, they stopped seeking the Giver.
That is why the presence of God matters more than the size of the territory.
Moses understood something similar when he told the Lord:
“If thy presence go not with me, carry us not up hence.”
— Exodus 33:15, KJV
Moses did not want to move forward without God's presence.
And Jabez's prayer gives us a reason to examine our own ambitions.
Are we asking God to accompany us in obedience?
Or are we asking Him to endorse plans we have never surrendered to Him?
Those are not the same thing.
You can pray over an opportunity without ever asking whether it honors Christ.
You can ask God to bless a relationship while refusing to obey His Word within it.
You can ask Him to prosper your work while ignoring dishonesty in the way you conduct it.
But the hand of God is not a religious decoration we place over our personal desires.
We are called to trust Him, obey Him, and seek His will.
And sometimes the most merciful thing God does is stop us from going somewhere we were convinced we needed to go.
Then comes the final request.
“...and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me!”
This part of the prayer carries an especially moving connection with Jabez's name.
The Hebrew includes:
וְעָשִׂיתָ מֵּרָעָה לְבִלְתִּי עָצְבִּי
Vəʿāśîtā mē­rāʿāh ləviltî ʿāṣbî.
The wording is compact and has been translated in different ways.
It expresses a request involving protection from evil or harm, so that pain or distress will not overtake him.
The final Hebrew word, ʿāṣbî, echoes the language of pain associated with his name.
Do you see the literary connection?
The man whose name was tied to sorrow asks God to protect him from sorrow.
The man whose birth was remembered through pain calls upon the Lord concerning the pain that might lie ahead.
It is as though the story brings his name and his prayer face-to-face.
But we must be careful.
The Bible does not say Jabez was trying to break a generational curse.
It does not say his name carried supernatural power to condemn him.
It does not tell us that his mother had spoken a spiritual sentence over his future.
Those ideas may sound dramatic, but they go beyond what Scripture reveals.
What the text actually gives us is already powerful enough.
A man associated with sorrow turned to God in prayer.
And God heard him.
That is not a magical formula.
It is a testimony of divine mercy.
And perhaps this is where the story touches the places we normally hide.
Because some of us are not afraid of failure anymore.
We are afraid of being hurt again.
We have survived things we never expected to survive.
We have buried dreams.
Trusted people who betrayed us.
Prayed beside hospital beds.
Stared at unanswered messages.
Sat in church while quietly wondering why God seemed so distant.
And after enough disappointment, the heart begins protecting itself.
You stop hoping too much.
Stop trusting too quickly.
Stop telling people what you are carrying.
Sometimes you even stop praying honestly.
Not because you have stopped believing God exists.
But because you are exhausted from feeling disappointed.
Jabez reminds us that we do not have to pretend pain is insignificant before bringing it to God.
We can ask for protection.
We can ask for help.
We can ask for blessing.
We can admit that we are afraid.
We can bring the very thing that hurts us into the presence of the One who knows us completely.
And still, we must remember that God has not promised every believer freedom from earthly suffering.
Jesus told His disciples:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.”
— John 16:33, KJV
Not you might have tribulation.
“You shall have tribulation.”
The Christian hope is not that suffering becomes impossible.
It is that suffering does not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
And now we arrive at the sentence that closes Jabez's entire recorded story.
“And God granted him that which he requested.”
That is all.
The writer does not describe the celebration.
He does not tell us how much land Jabez received.
He does not explain how the blessing unfolded or what happened afterward.
He simply records that God granted his request.
Then the genealogy continues.
And this is where the story becomes unforgettable.
For two verses, we encounter a man whose name was associated with pain, whose character was described as honorable, and whose prayer was answered by God.
Then he disappears from the biblical narrative.
No monument is described.
No extended biography follows.
No detailed list of achievements is preserved.
Yet thousands of years later, believers are still reading his prayer.
Not because Jabez became the center of the biblical story.
But because his brief appearance directs our attention toward the God who hears.
And perhaps that is precisely the perspective we need.
You do not need to become famous for your life to matter before God.
You do not need a massive audience.
A recognizable name.
An impressive title.
A perfect family history.
You can live an ordinary life, pray in an ordinary room, obey God in ordinary circumstances, and still have a life of extraordinary significance in His sight.
But there is an even greater truth waiting beyond the story of Jabez.
Because if we stop with Jabez, we have not yet reached the heart of the Gospel.
Jabez prayed that God would keep him from pain.
Jesus Christ entered a world of pain willingly.
Jabez asked for God's hand to be with him.
Jesus, the eternal Son of God, came in the flesh to accomplish the Father's saving purpose.
Jabez asked for blessing.
Christ became the source of the greatest blessing sinners could ever receive: reconciliation with God.
And here is where the contrast becomes deeply personal.
Jabez's name was associated with sorrow surrounding his birth.
Jesus was described by the prophet Isaiah as:
“...a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief...”
— Isaiah 53:3, KJV
But Jesus did not merely experience human sorrow.
He bore our sins.
Isaiah declares:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
— Isaiah 53:5, KJV
This prophecy finds its fulfillment in the suffering and saving work of Jesus Christ, who bore our sins and secured our reconciliation with God.
And consider the difference.
Jabez cried out because he wanted to be spared from harm.
Jesus prayed in Gethsemane:
“...nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.”
— Matthew 26:39, KJV
Jesus did not escape the cross.
He obeyed the Father through it.
He was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
He endured the judgment our sins deserved, not because He had sinned, but because He came to save sinners.
And on the third day, He rose from the dead.
That is the center of our hope.
Not that every earthly request will be granted.
Not that every painful memory will disappear.
Not that our bank accounts will always increase.
But that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Through Him, forgiveness is offered to sinners.
Through Him, the guilty can be justified by faith.
Through Him, those who were far from God can be brought near.
And through Him, the final destiny of everyone who belongs to Him is not condemnation, but eternal life.
This is what makes the Gospel more glorious than a story about personal improvement.
Jesus did not come merely to help wounded people become more successful.
He came to save sinners.
Including the ones who have learned to hide their sins behind religious language.
Including the ones who know how to raise their hands in worship but cannot remember the last time they truly surrendered their hearts.
Including the ones who have hurt others and spent years pretending they were only victims.
Including the ones who feel so ashamed of their past that they cannot imagine being forgiven.
The Gospel does not tell us that our sin is harmless.
It tells us that God's grace is greater than the debt we could never repay.
And that grace does not leave us unchanged.
It calls us to repentance.
To turn away from sin.
To abandon our self-righteousness.
To trust in the crucified and risen Savior.
To follow Him.
There is a difference between wanting Jesus to improve your circumstances and surrendering to Jesus as Lord.
One asks, “Lord, will You give me what I want?”
The other asks, “Lord, teach me to want what honors You.”
One is interested in His gifts.
The other is learning to treasure Him.
And perhaps that is the question this ancient prayer is placing before us.
If God enlarged your territory tomorrow, would your heart become more devoted to Christ?
If He increased your income, would you become more generous?
If He gave you influence, would you speak the truth with greater courage and humility?
If He opened the door you have been praying about, would you walk through it in obedience?
And if He did not grant the request, would you still trust His goodness?
That last question may be the hardest.
Because faith is not proven only when prayers are answered the way we hoped.
Sometimes faith is revealed when we continue clinging to Christ while tears are still falling.
Maybe you are reading this from a hospital room.
Maybe you are waiting for a child to come home.
Maybe your marriage is quietly falling apart.
Maybe you have been battling a private sin for years, promising God that this would be the last time.
Maybe you are carrying a grief nobody knows about because you have become the person everyone else depends on.
Or maybe your life looks completely normal from the outside.
You smile.
You work.
You serve.
You post encouraging verses.
You tell people you are blessed.
But there is a part of you that has been spiritually exhausted for a very long time.
And the question you are afraid to ask is whether God still wants to hear from you.
Listen carefully.
You do not have to become impressive before you come to Jesus.
You do not have to manufacture a beautiful prayer.
You do not have to hide the ugliness of your sin or the depth of your grief.
Come to Him truthfully.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Repent of what needs to be abandoned.
Ask for the mercy you cannot earn.
Trust the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
And remember His promise:
“...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
— John 6:37, KJV
Those words are not a guarantee that every circumstance will immediately change.
They are an invitation to come to the One who can save you.
And there is no greater transformation than being brought from spiritual death into life through Jesus Christ.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
— 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
Not because our past never happened.
Not because the consequences of sin automatically disappear.
Not because every earthly relationship will be restored.
But because in Christ, the past no longer has the authority to define our standing before God.
The sinner can be forgiven.
The proud can be humbled.
The brokenhearted can find comfort.
The wandering can repent and return.
The believer can be renewed in faith and obedience.
And the life that once seemed entirely defined by shame can become a testimony to the mercy of Jesus Christ.
That is not positive thinking.
That is the transforming power of the Gospel.
And if something in this story has touched a place you rarely talk about, I want to invite you to do something simple.
Be honest before God.
Not performative.
Not dramatic.
Just honest.
Or, if you are comfortable, share a few words of your testimony.
Not because a comment earns God's attention.
Not because public confession is required for forgiveness.
And certainly not because you owe strangers the details of your wounds.
But because your words may encourage another believer who thought they were struggling alone.
Someone may read your testimony tonight and find the courage to pray again.
Someone may discover that repentance is possible.
Someone may be reminded that God's mercy has not run out.
Send it privately to a family member who needs the reminder that Christ is greater than their past.
You may never know what God does through a Scripture-filled message placed before someone at the right moment.
Not as a lucky charm.
Not as a formula for obtaining blessings.
But as a reminder to return to Scripture when your prayers feel weak and your circumstances seem louder than God's promises.
Because one emotional moment is not the same as lifelong discipleship.
We need Scripture when life is beautiful.
And we need Scripture when life is unbearable.
We need truth that corrects us, grace that humbles us, and fellow believers who encourage us to remain faithful.
We want these resources to help people open their Bibles, understand the Gospel more clearly, strengthen their faith, and develop habits of spiritual growth.

Some believers choose to support Gospel-centered ministries as part of their regular giving and offerings. If you choose to do that here, we receive it with gratitude and a commitment to steward that support responsibly.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That is the kind of support we desire.
Willing.
Thoughtful.
Cheerful.
Free from pressure.
God is not selling His grace.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
Salvation is the free gift of God through Jesus Christ.
These products are simply another way to keep Scripture, encouragement, and meaningful reminders of faith close in everyday life.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read, learn, pray, share, and grow.
You can still explore the free resources.
You can still encourage this ministry by inviting others to follow.
It is good news to be proclaimed freely.
Perhaps it is by opening your Bible tonight.
Reading 1 Chronicles 4:9–10 for yourself.
Then turning to the Gospels.
Looking at the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus.
And asking the question that matters more than whether your territory becomes larger:
“Lord Jesus, does my life truly belong to You?”
Because one day, the possessions we accumulated will no longer matter.
The applause will fade.
The online numbers will disappear.
The titles we worked so hard to earn will lose their importance.
And what will matter eternally is whether we belong to Jesus Christ.
Jabez had only two verses recorded about him.
Yet his prayer still speaks.
Your life may never be recorded in a history book.
Your name may never be known by thousands.
But the God who heard Jabez is not limited by the obscurity of the person praying.
And through Jesus Christ, we have an even greater reason to approach God with confidence.
Hebrews 4:16 tells believers to come boldly to the throne of grace, to obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
So come.
Come with your fear.
Come with your repentance.
Come with the questions you cannot answer.
Come with the wounds you are tired of hiding.
Come with your hopes, but surrender them to God's wisdom.
Come asking not merely for a larger life, but for a heart that belongs wholly to Christ.
And if you cannot find the words tonight, perhaps begin here:
“Father, I have carried things that have shaped the way I see myself. Some were done to me. Others were the result of my own sinful choices. You know the truth about all of them.
Forgive my sins through Jesus Christ. Teach me to repent where I have rebelled against You. Heal what is wounded according to Your wisdom, and help me obey You even where healing takes time.
Bless me in the ways that truly honor You. Give me opportunities to serve others faithfully. Let Your hand guide me, protect me from evil, and keep my heart from wandering away from Your Word.
And if my circumstances do not change as quickly as I hope, remind me that Your grace is still sufficient.
Let my life tell the truth about Jesus, not merely about what I have survived.
In His holy name, amen.”
And now, before you leave this story behind, remember the man whose name meant so much more to the people around him than we can fully reconstruct.
Jabez did not get to choose the circumstances of his birth.
He did not get to erase the sorrow associated with his name.
But the Bible remembers him as honorable, as a man who called upon God, and as someone whose request God granted.
We should not add to his story what Scripture has not revealed.
And we should not miss what Scripture has made clear.
The Lord heard him.
And the same Scriptures lead us beyond Jabez to Jesus Christ, whose cross and resurrection provide a hope no painful history can cancel for those who trust in Him.
So do not make your wound your savior.
Do not make your success your identity.
Do not make an answered prayer the foundation of your faith.
Build your life on Jesus.
He is greater than the pain you remember.
Greater than the shame you carry.
Greater than the sin you must repent of.
Greater than the future you fear.
And when you find yourself tempted to believe that the worst chapter of your life is the only chapter that matters, remember the Gospel.
The world may remember the name they gave your pain, but in Christ, your pain does not get to pronounce the final word over your eternity.
